data.title: Považská Bystrica – Šibeničný vŕšok, a Púchov culture promontory hillfort
data.excerpt: In the cadastral area of Považská Bystrica, archaeologists confirmed a fortified promontory hillfort of the Púchov culture in the locality known as “Hradište”, also called “Šibeničný vŕšok”. A ditch 6–8 m wide and more than 2.5 m deep cut off the ridge, while several dozen flint and radiolarite flakes outside the defences point to far older, Palaeolithic activity on the spur.

children.text: In the cadastral area of Považská Bystrica, archaeologists succeeded in confirming the existence of a fortified promontory hillfort of the Púchov culture in the locality known as “Hradište” (also called “Šibeničný vŕšok”).

In one part of the hillfort, isolated traces of a later occupation of the site were also recorded (linear trenches, sunken pits and the like), without any possibility of more precise dating. In a stretch some 50 to 100 metres from the fortification, on the outer (SW) side of the hillfort, the archaeologists recorded during the excavation the occurrence of flakes of flint and radiolarite, of which several dozen pieces were found. For this reason they carried out an area excavation at these spots, in order to establish whether these finds came from the ploughsoil or signalled finds at greater depths. According to the preliminary results of the excavation, this is evidence of the use of the site in the Old Stone Age (Palaeolithic). Numerous miniature chips document the production of stone tools on the spot.

children.text: The locality known as “Hradište” is an elongated ridge above the Váh valley, oriented roughly NE – SW. On the northern, eastern and southern sides the site is protected by steep slopes. The south-western side of the spur was cut off by a ditch 6–8 m wide and more than 2.5 m deep. Above the ditch an
was piled up. On the outer side of the rampart there was a
drystone wall reinforced with wooden posts

. The rampart was not visible on the ground, because it had been spread out by ploughing. The excavation showed that part of the body of the rampart slid back into the ditch after the front wall collapsed. The ditch itself reinforced above all the highest part of the ridge, where it followed the course of the rampart. In the southern and northern parts it petered out freely in lower-lying terrain. In the northern part of the ridge the situation on the ground had been destroyed by a massive landslide at the edge of the slope. In the south-eastern, lower-lying part of the hillfort the fortification turned in a south-easterly direction into the area of today’s private plots. On the southern side the excavation managed to uncover the probable
entrance into the fortified enclosure of the hillfort
. From the eastern and NE sides the site was protected by a steep slope.

children.text: The occupation layer was relatively thin – about 20 to 40 cm. Besides sunken storage pits and an oven, remains of ground-level post-built structures were recorded. The larger number of post holes also attests to larger houses measuring 4 × 8 m, or possibly to the existence of an inner palisade. The occupation was not confined to the immediately fortified inner area of the recorded hillfort alone. On the southern side, in the area of today’s private plots (gardens), there are several horizontal terraces on the slope, ending in a steep slope above the Jelšové part of Považská Bystrica. The first occupation, datable to the 1st century BC, apparently came to an end in a fire. The post-built structures with walls daubed with clay were apparently rebuilt after the turn of the era. The end of occupation at the site can provisionally be dated to the 1st – 2nd century AD. There are relatively few finds from the occupation layer across the area of the hillfort. Metal objects are almost entirely absent. The excavation of the hillfort contributed to our insights into the occupation of the Považská Bystrica region at the turn of the era and added to our insights into the life of the people of the Púchov culture in this part of Slovakia. The evidence that people stayed in this area in the Old Stone Age is also of great importance.
